claims.text: DNS is the naming system that turns a name into an IP address by asking machines whose job is to hold the answer.
claims.source_hint: RFC 1034 section 2.3 and section 3 — the domain name system as a distributed name-to-resource mapping queried through name servers

claims.text: A resolver answers the question of which address a name has, and each machine is configured with a list of resolvers to ask, usually handed to it by the network it connects to.
claims.source_hint: RFC 1034 section 5.3.1 — a stub resolver needs a list of name server addresses, held in a configuration file (/etc/resolv.conf on the lab box)

claims.text: A record is one stored line of an answer; the kind this lesson uses pairs a name with an address. One name may have several records and one address may be reached by several names.
claims.source_hint: RFC 1034 sections 3.6 and 3.6.2 — resource records, several address records for one name, and aliases pointing at one name

claims.text: A time-to-live is stated together with a record: the length of time for which whoever receives that record may keep using it before asking again.
claims.source_hint: RFC 1035 section 3.2.1 — the TTL field of a resource record, the interval it may be kept before the source is consulted again

claims.text: The machine's ordinary name lookup reads the hosts file before any resolver is asked, and a name listed there is answered from the file without asking anyone; some tools, `nslookup` among them, skip the file and ask a resolver directly.
claims.source_hint: POSIX getaddrinfo() and the nsswitch.conf hosts line (`files dns`) — the local file is consulted ahead of DNS; hosts(5); nslookup(1) queries name servers directly

claims.text: At tag stage-0 the lab box's hosts file pairs `donhang.local` with `127.0.0.1`, written there by the lab's own configuration, and `STAGE.md` asks the learner to add the identical line on their own machine before that name opens in a browser.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang docker-compose.yml at stage-0 (service lab, extra_hosts "donhang.local:127.0.0.1") and STAGE.md; outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/resolve.txt

claims.text: Inside the lab the resolver is run by the lab itself and holds the names of the machines on the lab network, answering `db` with `172.28.0.11` and `lab` with `172.28.0.12`.
claims.source_hint: Docker docs, user-defined bridge networks — the embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11 resolves container and service names; examples/don-hang docker-compose.yml ipam addresses at stage-0

claims.text: For every name there are name servers whose job is to hold the true answer for it, normally more than one, so the answer survives a machine going down; that is also where the answer is changed when a name is pointed at another machine.
claims.source_hint: RFC 1034 sections 4.1 and 4.3.2 — every zone required on at least two servers; the authoritative servers for a zone hold its data, which is where a name's answer is changed

claims.text: A resolver may keep an answer for the time-to-live that came with it and give that same answer to later askers without asking again, so an answer received may be older than the moment it is given out.
claims.source_hint: RFC 1034 section 3.6 and section 4.3.4 — storing answers for the TTL and answering from what is stored

claims.text: `nslookup` asks a resolver and prints the answer that comes back.
claims.source_hint: nslookup(1) man page — query internet name servers interactively; outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/resolve.txt in the example repository

claims.text: `nslookup` queries a resolver directly and does not read the machine's hosts file, so a name listed only in that file, such as `donhang.local` on the lab box, gets no answer from the resolver that box uses.
claims.source_hint: nslookup(1) — queries name servers directly, not the host resolution libraries; execution on the lab box at stage-0: nslookup donhang.local against getent hosts donhang.local

claims.text: At stage-0 the lab box's hosts file holds `localhost` (plus `ip6-localhost`, `ip6-loopback`), four further fixed names the system puts there, `donhang.local` at `127.0.0.1` and `donhang-lab` at `172.28.0.12`; neither `db` nor `lab` appears, so both of those answers came from the resolver.
claims.source_hint: outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/resolve.txt — the full /etc/hosts listing printed by the script's last line

claims.text: `NXDOMAIN` is how a resolver reports that the name asked about does not exist; the script's third question, `no-such-host.donhang`, is answered that way.
claims.source_hint: RFC 1035 section 4.1.1 — RCODE 3, Name Error, meaning the domain name does not exist; outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/resolve.txt

claims.text: A name that does not exist and a machine that exists with nothing listening on the asked port are two different outcomes: the first fails before any connection is tried.
claims.source_hint: RFC 1035 section 4.1.1 (Name Error) against RFC 9293 section 3.5.2 (reset for a connection to a port in CLOSED state) — different layers, different failures

claims.text: At stage-0 the lab box's hosts file lists `172.28.0.12` under the name `donhang-lab`, the same address the resolver gives for the name `lab`: one address reached by two names.
claims.source_hint: outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/resolve.txt; examples/don-hang docker-compose.yml at stage-0 (service lab, hostname donhang-lab, ipv4_address 172.28.0.12)

claims.text: A resolver's stored answer is counted from the moment that resolver received it, not from the moment the name's owner changed the record, which is why a change is seen at different times from different machines.
claims.source_hint: RFC 1034 section 4.3.4 and RFC 1035 section 3.2.1 — the TTL is decremented from the time the entry was stored by that server

claims.text: The lines in a hosts file are local to the machine that holds them, so a name resolved from that file on one machine resolves nowhere else unless the same line is added there too.
claims.source_hint: hosts(5) — the file is a local static table of name-to-address entries for that host only

claims.text: A resolver asked for a name it does not hold asks those name servers on the asker's behalf, working down the chain towards the ones that hold the name, and passes the answer back.
claims.source_hint: RFC 1034 sections 4.3.1 and 5.3.3 — recursive service, and the referrals a resolver follows towards the servers authoritative for the name

claims.text: Five of the eight lines in the lab box's hosts file at stage-0 write their addresses in the second notation (`::1`, `fe00::`, `ff00::`, `ff02::1`, `ff02::2`), which this lesson does not use.
claims.source_hint: outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/resolve.txt — the /etc/hosts listing printed by the script's last line; five of its eight lines use the second address notation

beyond_scope: One sentence in section 5 says that `nslookup` skips the hosts file and asks a resolver directly. It is not an outline item, but without it the script's own last line ("the file the machine reads before it asks any resolver") would leave the reader believing `nslookup` consulted that file.

open_questions: Outline item 2 has two halves. The half "several names can point to one address" is shown from the repository (`lab` and `donhang-lab` both reach 172.28.0.12). The other half, "a name can point to several addresses", has no evidence at stage-0 — no name in the lab is answered with more than one address — so it is stated as a fact of DNS (claim 3) and not demonstrated. A repository change adding a second address for one name would be out of proportion for one L1 lesson; flagging it rather than inventing a demonstration.
